Un mémorial en l'honneur d'Elisapee Poot: A memorial in honour of Elisapee Pootoogook, who died on November 13
Cette année, plusieurs femmes inuit de l: This year, several Inuit women from the Cabot Square community have died in Montréal. Several others are missing. The Inuit community watches winter approach with worry. It fears there won’t be enough resources to prevent more deaths. But why are so many women disappearing?
En novembre dernier, plusieurs membres d: Last November, several community members gathered and spoke out to commemorate those who lost their lives and to demand change, in the hope of avoiding another tragedy.
Le 12 novembre, sous une pluie torrentie: On November 12, in a torrential downpour, dozens of members of Inuit communities from across the country gathered to commemorate eight Inuit women from the Cabot Square community who have disappeared. In an atmosphere of sharing and protest, they discussed the importance of valuing the lives of Inuit women. Under tents decorated with traditional dresses, the women attending the event hugged and caught up with one another. An elder recited a prayer in Inuktitut to open the event. The crowd bowed their heads in silence, thinking of the missing. Poems written by Inuit women during a therapeutic writing exercise were read at the commemoration. Each one began with the words “I am…” and described its author.
Le but de ce projet, mené par l’Aborigin: The aim of the project, led by the Aboriginal Women’s Action Network (AWAN), was to help participants find their voice and be proud of who they are. “I am a mom, a former sex worker, a broken star,” one could hear in a silence punctuated by the sound of raindrops at Cabot Square. “I am Cree-Inuit. I am a survivor. I am a family. I am a friend. I am talkative. I am a grandmother. I am a mother. I am an elder.
J’ai 53 ans. » En ce jour de commémorati: I am 53 years old.” On this day of remembrance, Anita is thinking of her loved ones. “I knew most of the eight women who died. One of them was my cousin. It’s still too hard for me to talk about it,” she says, her voice breaking. In her grief, she finds comfort in the presence of everyone who came out to support her despite the bad weather. She hopes that missing and murdered Inuit women, like her cousin, will not be forgotten. Anita, who has lived in Montréal for 15 years, knows how hard it can be for them to adapt to the city. She is nevertheless happy to be surrounded by people today. “I was able to find a community at the Native friendship centre, where I met women I could talk with.
Je me suis fait de très bonnes amies et: I made some really good friends and I still meet people there,” she says. She hopes to keep meeting with others so she can carry the voices of her Inuit sisters. Kira, a mother, shares the many projects she has in mind. “I’m involved in a healthy eating program for Inuit women. I want all of us to have access to our traditional food,” says the woman, who prefers not to reveal her real identity because of an ongoing legal dispute.
Elle s’illumine en parlant du programme: She lights up when talking about the horseback riding program for Indigenous people that she dreams of setting up. “Every time I meet Indigenous people, they eagerly ask me when the program will start. It’s good to have so much support,” she says happily. In the middle of our conversation, Kira breaks off to call out to a young woman heading toward the metro station. The two women embrace for a long time. After exchanging a few words with her friend and saying goodbye, Kira comes back to us. “I’m so glad she’s alive. I found her; her family had asked me to look for her. I’m going to tell her sister the good news,” she says, crying, visibly relieved after several months without word. One of the young woman’s sisters is also missing. The last time the friend’s loved ones heard from her was a few months ago. They saw her pimp threaten her with death on social media before she deleted her Facebook account. “The disappearance of our loved ones is something we Inuit women have to live with every day,” Kira laments. “We really need to make non-Indigenous people aware of this reality,” she says of the disappearances.
Fay Blaney, cofondatrice de l’Aboriginal: Fay Blaney, cofounder of the Aboriginal Women’s Action Network (AWAN), a collective of Indigenous feminist women, took part in the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls. That experience made her understand the scale of the danger facing Inuit women who die on the street. “Every time one of these deaths is covered in the media, they say the woman had a dangerous lifestyle. The media don’t listen, they devalue her and erase her story. We don’t want this to happen again,” she says. Ms. Blaney, who has headed AWAN since 1995, wants to give Inuit women back the reins of their own lives. She organizes feminist workshops to inform them about certain systemic issues and equip them to face those issues.
Lors des commémorations, on peut voir qu: At the commemoration, the women’s demands can be seen on a drawing of a tree set up under a tent. Among other things, they call for Inuit foster families for their children and an end to birth alerts, which notify the authorities every time an Inuit baby is born. “We want these women to find their voice and control their future, instead of someone else doing it for them. When they have a voice, they can be the architects of their own lives,” says Ms. Blaney, full of hope.
Le lendemain de l’événement commémoratif: The day after the commemorative event at Cabot Square, Elisapee Pootoogook, a 61-year-old Inuit grandmother, died at the construction site of a luxury condo on René-Lévesque Boulevard, very close to Cabot Square, the Inuit gathering place. Her loved ones tell us Elisapee had come to Montréal for five days to receive health care. Her health was fragile and she only wanted to find a warm place to sleep. Every time the grandmother took refuge in the metro, security made her leave, on the pretext that loitering in the metro posed a risk of spreading COVID-19.
La nuit fatale, ayant épuisé toutes les: On the fatal night, having run out of options, Elisapee went a little farther than usual to sleep. She lost her life there. The tragedy sparked an outcry in the Inuit community and beyond. Her death reignited the conversation about Indigenous homelessness in Montréal.
Le lundi 22 novembre, des dizaines de pe: On Monday, November 22, dozens of people gathered in her memory at Cabot Square, a place Elisapee frequented. Makivik Corporation, an organization that represents Inuit interests with Québec City and Ottawa, sent an invitation letter to Mayor Valérie Plante and her office, as well as to the Minister responsible for Indigenous Affairs, Ian Lafrenière. Neither showed up, an absence that angered many community members. The next day, Ronald Coolem, Elisapee’s son-in-law, and his Montréal family flew to the Far North with the body of the deceased.
Tous ensemble, ils y ont tenu une cérémo: There, all together, they held a ceremony in memory of the Inuit elder. “Her husband is waiting for her. The little ones, who are two and five, are asking when grandma is coming home,” he told us.
M. Coolem s’est dit très déçu de l’absen: Mr. Coolem said he was very disappointed by the politicians’ absence from the Montréal commemoration. “It’s something you can’t hide. We’re just going to lose even more people this winter,” he said after the event.
Il a trouvé inacceptable que sa belle-mè: He found it unacceptable that his mother-in-law, who had come to Montréal for five days to receive health care, ended her days this way. He was outraged that Indigenous people are treated like this. During the ceremony, Lizzie Puttayuk, the deceased’s niece, spoke.
Sur scène, elle a ouvert une Bible pour: On stage, she opened a Bible to recite a prayer in Inuktitut. “I prayed for her to rest in peace. At the same time, I want to send a message to her family to reassure them and tell them that another world exists,” she confided to us after the event.
Lizzie Puttayuk, nièce d’Elisapee Pootoo: Lizzie Puttayuk, niece of Elisapee Pootoogook. Photo: Diamond Yao
Mme Puttayuk s’est souvenue de sa tante: Ms. Puttayuk remembered her aunt as someone overflowing with kindness who treated everyone with respect. She admired her excellent English and her Scrabble skills. Her death came as an enormous shock. She too was outraged that her aunt died in such conditions.
« Moi, je ne peux pas vivre dans le Nord: “I can’t live in the North, so I stay in Montréal. Why is it so hard to give us a roof in Montréal?
Je n’aime pas vivre dans des refuges »,: I don’t like living in shelters,” she said with frustration, explaining that she can’t sleep well in shelters, or else she has to wake up very early in the cold. “We have the right to be healthy and safe.”
<strong>Qu’est-ce que la Ville prévoit f: What does the City plan to do?
Questionnée à ce sujet, Marikym Gaudreau: Asked about this, Marikym Gaudreault, Valérie Plante’s press secretary, replied that her office had not been informed of the tribute to Elisapee Pootoogook on November 22. Ms. Gaudreault also said she was unaware that at least nine Inuit women had died this year, adding that her office had recorded only one missing woman. The right to be healthy and safe is what Montréal’s Inuit community is asking for. In response, the mayor’s office says it is working on deploying a new resource.
« On veut un refuge permanent pour les p: “We want a permanent shelter for Indigenous people, one that is culturally adapted and heated, near Cabot Square. We are currently in discussions with the provincial government,” Ms. Gaudreault told us. She confirms that a permanent shelter for Indigenous and Inuit people will open by the end of the fall. The city administration has doubled funding for homelessness issues, from $3 million to $6 million. It also plans to build 1,200 housing units for people experiencing homelessness, including units for Indigenous people and 23 units for Indigenous women and their children. Another portion of the money will go to community groups fighting homelessness. The City’s initiatives were well received by several members of the Inuit community. “That’s fantastic!” Kira exclaims on learning that a permanent Indigenous shelter will open by the start of winter. “I’d heard about it, but I wasn’t sure the project would actually happen.” Joey Partridge, a member of the Southern Quebec Inuit Association, also receives the news with optimism. “Yes, 1,200 more housing units is a good start. I think it will really help people,” he says. “But I want to see it with my own eyes before I celebrate.” He hopes the new shelter will offer cultural activities in Inuktitut and other Indigenous languages.
L’intervenant est également heureux que: The community worker is also happy that the mayor finally agreed to meet with him on December 6 to discuss issues affecting Inuit. “The director of the Southern Quebec Inuit Association has really made a lot of effort to get governments to listen to Inuit demands,” he says. “But there was no progress until very recently, when people started to understand that there were a lot of Inuit on the street.”
Serge Sasseville, conseiller de ville du: Serge Sasseville, city councillor for the Peter-McGill district and a member of the opposition, reportedly did not receive an invitation, according to his party’s press secretary. Benoît Langevin, Ensemble Montréal’s spokesperson on homelessness, says he would have liked to be there. He is critical of the Plante administration. “How is it that, for four years now, when temperatures hit -20 oC, we still haven’t put winter measures in place for people experiencing homelessness?” In his view, the difficulty in finding a permanent location for an Inuit shelter stems from downtown Montréal’s zoning rules. “Property owners in Ville-Marie don’t want rooming houses and shelters near their properties because it would lower their property value,” Mr. Langevin explains. He denounces the fact that many homeless people have nowhere to sleep at night because of public health measures that reduce shelter capacity, and because many resources are not open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
Le porte-parole nous parle longuement de: The spokesperson spoke at length about issues specific to Montréal’s Inuit community, including the lack of health services in the North and the lack of psychosocial support. Mr. Langevin has not, however, spoken with Résilience Montréal or the Native Women’s Shelter of Montreal, organizations that serve Montréal’s Inuit community. Minister Lafrenière and federal Minister of Crown-Indigenous Relations Marc Miller both declined our interview requests.
Alisha Tukkiapik, membre de Québec solid: Alisha Tukkiapik, a member of Québec solidaire and a former provincial election candidate, wants to demystify the reasons Inuit women move to Montréal. “What people don’t understand is that it has nothing to do with alcohol and drugs. Inuit women leave Nunavik because of the lack of infrastructure and services,” she says. “There is a serious shortage of adequate housing in the Far North. These women come south to rest from a life where they are crammed into tiny housing,” Ms. Tukkiapik explains. She laments that all three levels of government fail to understand the harshness of the Arctic’s social and environmental climate and provide poorly built, ill-suited housing that deteriorates easily. In 2014, <l1>a report</l1> by the Société d’habitation du Québec concluded that there was a shortage of 899 social housing units in Nunavik.
Il y aurait, entre autres, un manque de: There is reportedly, among other things, a lack of housing for families. On this point, $250 million will be allocated for infrastructure in Nunavik from 2018 to 2028, Nicolas Moquin, communications advisor at Indigenous Services Canada, told us. Mr. Moquin does not mention what measures the government plans to put in place to address housing construction problems. Ms. Tukkiapik is extremely critical of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. “People want to talk about reconciliation, but we haven’t even finished talking about the truths. And the truth is that not enough resources are allocated to us, on the pretext that there’s no budget,” she says indignantly.
La politicienne souhaite que des investi: The politician wants ambitious investments in education and health care for Inuit. “We have a lot of intergenerational trauma and we don’t have access to help to heal. That’s why there is a suicide epidemic in our communities,” she believes. Janis Qavavauq-Bibeau, a front-line worker at the <l1>Native Women’s Shelter of Montreal</l1>, says several factors push Inuit women to leave the Far North for the south. Besides the housing crisis, there is access to medical care, the reason Elisapee was in Montréal. During their stays, those who can’t afford lodging turn to organizations that host Inuit travelling for medical reasons.
« Le problème, c’est que dans ces organi: “The problem is that in these organizations, you can’t drink alcohol. That rule doesn’t take into account the historical realities of Inuit people. Many drink because a lot of harm was done to them in the past,” explains Ms. Qavavauq-Bibeau, who is fed up with the prejudice and stigma surrounding alcohol and Inuit.
Elle souligne la nécessité d’avoir des r: She stresses the need for resources for people who use substances, and for an intervention approach that supports people while respecting their lived experience. To illustrate the tragedies that mark multiple generations, the front-line worker cites residential schools, whose legacy left intergenerational scars on most members of Inuit communities, and <l1>the slaughter of sled dogs by law enforcement in the 1950s</l1>, among others. For Inuit, who relied on their dogs to survive, the slaughter marked the end of their nomadic way of life and the beginning of their dependence on the government. She reminds us that the roots of the problems must be tackled, that is, the wrongs committed by Canadian institutions.
Mme Qavavauq-Bibeau croit également qu’i: Ms. Qavavauq-Bibeau also believes that health care adapted to Inuit realities is necessary, and that adapted mental health care is very hard to access, both in the Far North and in Montréal.
<strong>Pouvoir vivre dignement au nord: Being able to live with dignity in the North and the South
De nombreux obstacles se dressent dans l: Many obstacles stand in the way of Inuit women arriving in the city from their northern communities. Mr. Partridge, of the Southern Quebec Inuit Association, believes that interventions to protect these women must begin as soon as they arrive. His organization wants to partner with airports and hospitals so it can inform newcomers. “We want them to know where the women’s shelters, housing, churches and Indigenous and Inuit organizations are that they can turn to for support in Montréal,” he says. He hopes to set up a similar initiative in Nunavik, so women can better plan their stay.
Il souhaite obtenir le soutien des diffé: He wants the support of the different levels of government to open an Inuit cultural centre in Montréal that would offer various programs in Inuktitut and be staffed by Inuit. “Women would then have a place to go to find people who understand their language and their realities,” he says. On top of the lack of a fixed address and the danger of pimps, there are difficulties related to the language barrier, culture, and a lack of education and work experience, which make women who leave their communities to settle in Montréal even more vulnerable.
Mme Qavavauq-Bibeau propose que des soin: Ms. Qavavauq-Bibeau proposes that basic care be offered to Inuit women in the North as much as in the South, along with housing and healthy food. “That would give them a certain stability. They also need programs that accompany them and offer psychological support.”
En attendant les mesures gouvernementale: While waiting for government measures, Janis Qavavauq-Bibeau and Alisha Tukkiapik end on the same thought: systemic racism must be recognized by the provincial government for things to move forward.
« Je veux qu’ils arrêtent de nier le rac: “I want them to stop denying systemic racism. The denial hurts us. We want concrete solutions,” says Ms. Tukkiapik. Such recognition, according to Ms. Qavavauq-Bibeau, would give hope to all Inuit women.
Le gouvernement fédéral prévoit accorder: The federal government plans to grant $130 million to Makivik Corporation over the next four years. It also says that a funding agreement of more than $70 million over 10 years between Indigenous Services Canada and the Nunavik Regional Board of Health and Social Services (NRBHSS) was signed in 2019. A $129.5-million fund was also granted to Inuit last year to help them manage the health crisis.
En matière d’éducation, le gouvernement: On education, the Government of Canada is offering $150.6 million in funding over two years starting in 2021-2022 to help Indigenous students through the Post-Secondary Student Support Program and the Inuit and Métis Nation post-secondary education strategies. It is also providing $26.4 million in funding in 2021-2022 to Indigenous post-secondary institutions to help them deal with the pandemic through the Post-Secondary Partnerships Program and the Inuit and Métis Nation post-secondary education strategies. Nicolas Moquin, communications advisor at Indigenous Services Canada, says that, in addition to the mobilization efforts of the organization Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, an Inuit Post-Secondary Education Strategy has been put in place by the federal government. The strategy, valued at $147.3 million, supports Inuit students by providing financial assistance during their studies.
